c: Start with a water tank

Picture a tank on a tower with a pipe running down to a tap. The height of the tank sets how hard the water pushes. The width of the pipe sets how easily it flows. The stream coming out of the tap is the result of those two things together. Electricity behaves closely enough like this that engineers still use the picture. Voltage is the push. Resistance is how narrow the pipe is. Current is the flow that results. Nearly every question you will ask about a circuit is one of these three, hiding behind a part number or a symptom.
Voltage is a difference, not a place

Voltage, measured in volts, is the push between two points. It is always between two points, which is why a multimeter has two probes. A 9 volt battery does not have 9 volts in it. It has 9 volts across it, from one terminal to the other. A bird sits on a power line unharmed because both feet are at the same voltage, so nothing pushes current through the bird. When someone says a point in a circuit is at 5 volts, they mean 5 volts compared with ground, the point everyone agreed to call zero.
Current is what actually moves

Current, measured in amperes or amps, is how much charge passes a point each second. It is the thing that does the work and the thing that does the damage. An LED glows at about 0.02 amps, written 20 milliamps. A phone charger delivers 1 to 3 amps. A car starter motor pulls several hundred for a few seconds. Current only flows around a complete loop, out of the source, through the parts and back again. Break the loop anywhere and it stops everywhere at once, which is all a switch really does.
Resistance sets the price of flow

Resistance, measured in ohms, is how hard a material fights current. Copper wire fights very little, so a metre of hookup wire is a small fraction of an ohm. Rubber, glass and dry air fight so hard that almost nothing gets through. In between sit resistors, parts built to have a known value such as 220 or 10,000 ohms. Designers use them like valves, choosing how much current each branch of a circuit is allowed. Resistance turns electrical energy into heat, which is useful in a toaster and a nuisance nearly everywhere else.
How the three lock together

The three quantities are tied by one rule. For a given resistance, more voltage pushes more current. For a given voltage, more resistance allows less current. Put 9 volts across 450 ohms and 0.02 amps flows. Double the voltage and the current doubles. Double the resistance and the current halves. You never get to pick all three. Choose two and the circuit decides the third for you. That is why a part rated for 5 volts dies on 12: the higher push forces more current through it than it was built to carry.
Units and the prefixes you will meet

Electronics spans enormous ranges, so the units come with prefixes. Milli means a thousandth, micro a millionth. Kilo means a thousand, mega a million. A sensor might draw 50 microamps while the motor beside it draws 2 amps, forty thousand times more. A pull-up resistor might be 10 kilohms and a current sense resistor 10 milliohms. Getting the prefix wrong is the classic beginner error, and it is always wrong by a factor of a thousand. Say the unit out loud with its prefix every time and the mistake becomes much harder to make.
What to carry out of this

When a circuit confuses you, ask the three questions in order. Where is the push coming from, and how many volts is it? What path can current take to get back to the source? What on that path limits the flow? A dead circuit usually has no push or a broken path. A hot or smoking one usually has too little resistance on the path. Beginners often chase exotic explanations. People who fix things for a living start with these three, because most faults are one of them wearing a disguise.
A call is a bet at fixed odds

When an opponent bets, the pot is offering you a wager. You put in a known amount for the chance to win what is already out there. Pot odds are just that ratio: the money you can win compared with the money you must pay. Suppose the pot holds 100 dollars and your opponent bets 50. There is now 150 to win and it costs you 50 to try. You are getting 150 to 50, or 3 to 1. Nothing about your cards has entered the picture yet. This is purely the price.
Turn the price into a percentage

Odds of 3 to 1 mean that out of four tries, you can lose three and win one and break even. So you need to win one time in four, or 25 percent. The quick formula is the size of your call divided by the total pot after you call. Here that is 50 divided by 200, which is 25 percent. If your hand will win more often than that, calling makes money over time. If it will win less often, calling loses money, no matter how the hand feels.
Memorize four bet sizes

You do not need to calculate at the table if you learn the common cases. Facing a bet of one third of the pot, you need 20 percent. Facing half the pot, 25 percent. Facing two thirds, about 29 percent. Facing a bet the full size of the pot, 33 percent. A bet of twice the pot demands 40 percent. Notice how gently the requirement rises. Even a huge overbet never asks you to be a favourite. It only asks you to win often enough to pay for the times you lose.
A worked example with a draw

You hold two hearts and by the turn the board shows two more. One card is left to come, and nine hearts remain among the 46 cards you cannot see. You will complete the flush about 19.6 percent of the time on that last card. Your opponent bets 50 into 100, so you need 25 percent. A flush draw alone is not enough at that price. Had the bet been 25 into 100, you would need only one sixth, about 16.7 percent, and the call would be correct.
Why small bets are hard to fold to

Pot odds explain a feeling every player knows: small bets are annoying. A bet of a quarter of the pot offers 5 to 1, so you need to win barely 17 percent of the time. Many weak hands clear that bar. This is why good players do not fold everything to a tiny bet, and why betting small with a strong hand that wants a call is often correct. The size of the bet, as much as the cards, decides how wide the caller can profitably be.
What pot odds leave out

The basic sum assumes the hand ends after your call. Often it does not. If more cards and more bets are coming, you may win extra money when you hit, which improves the deal, or face another bet when you miss, which worsens it. Those adjustments have their own names, implied odds and reverse implied odds. Pot odds are the starting point: the honest price right now. Skilled players start there and then adjust for what is likely to happen on later streets.
Make it a habit

Before every call, say the price to yourself: what is in the pot, what does it cost, what percentage is that. Then ask how often your hand wins. Most losing players skip the first half and go straight to hoping. The habit takes a few sessions to become automatic, and it removes the most expensive leak in casual poker, which is calling too often with hands that cannot win enough of the time to justify the price.
The rule itself

Ohm's law says voltage equals current times resistance. Write it V equals I times R, where I is the old symbol for current. Rearranged, current is voltage divided by resistance, and resistance is voltage divided by current. Cover the one you want and the other two show you what to do. Twelve volts across 6 ohms gives 2 amps. Five volts pushing 0.5 amps means 10 ohms. Georg Ohm published the relationship in 1827 and was mocked for it. Nearly two centuries later it is the first thing anyone checks.
Think in milliamps and kilohms

Small circuits rarely deal in whole amps. They deal in milliamps, thousandths of an amp, and kilohms, thousands of ohms. Those two units cancel neatly. Volts divided by kilohms gives milliamps directly. Five volts across 10 kilohms is 0.5 milliamps. Three point three volts across 1 kilohm is 3.3 milliamps. Keep the units paired like that and you can do most bench arithmetic in your head. Mix amps with kilohms and you will be off by a factor of a thousand, the most common mistake a beginner makes.
The classic example: an LED

A red LED wants about 20 milliamps and drops about 2 volts when lit. You have a 5 volt supply. The resistor in series must soak up the other 3 volts while passing 20 milliamps. Three volts divided by 20 milliamps is 0.15 kilohms, or 150 ohms. The nearest common value above that is 220 ohms, which gives a slightly dimmer and longer lived LED. That thirty second calculation is the one you will do most often in hobby electronics, and it is nothing but Ohm's law applied to the leftover voltage.
Use it to find faults

Ohm's law also works backwards as a detective. If a resistor marked 100 ohms measures 4 volts across it, 40 milliamps must be flowing through it, whether or not the design intended that. Measuring voltage across a known resistance is how technicians find current without cutting a wire. If the number is far from what the design expects, something upstream is wrong. A voltage that should be there and is not, or a current that is much too high, points you toward the fault faster than staring at the board.
Where the law runs out

Ohm's law describes parts whose resistance stays put, such as resistors and wires. Many parts do not behave that way. A diode passes almost nothing until about 0.6 volts and then conducts freely. A light bulb filament has ten times more resistance hot than cold. A transistor changes its resistance on command, which is the whole point of it. For those parts you still use the law, but on one operating point at a time, with numbers taken from the datasheet, not from one fixed resistance.
The same law explains wire sizes

Wire has resistance too, small but real. A thin wire carrying a large current loses voltage along its length, and the loss is current times the wire's resistance. Ten amps through a cable with a tenth of an ohm of resistance drops a full volt before the power reaches the load, and the cable warms up doing it. That is why jumper cables are as thick as a thumb, why long runs of low voltage garden lighting dim at the far end, and why electricians choose wire gauge by the current it must carry.
A habit worth building

Before you connect power to anything, estimate the current. Take the supply voltage, divide by the smallest resistance on the path, and ask whether the answer is reasonable. Five volts into 220 ohms is about 23 milliamps, fine. Five volts into a wire with nothing else on the path is whatever the supply can deliver, which means a short circuit. The estimate takes five seconds and saves parts, batteries and fingertips. People who do this every time rarely see smoke. People who skip it meet smoke early and often.
What an out is

An out is any unseen card that turns your hand into the likely winner. If you hold four cards to a flush, there are thirteen cards of that suit in the deck, you can see four, so nine remain. Those nine are your outs. An open-ended straight draw, such as 8 and 9 on a board of 7, 10 and a king, can be completed by any six or any jack: eight outs. A gutshot, needing one specific rank in the middle, has four. Counting outs is the first step in knowing what a draw is worth.
The shortcut

With one card to come, multiply your outs by two to get the approximate percentage chance of hitting. With two cards to come, on the flop, multiply by four. A flush draw with nine outs has roughly 18 percent on the next card and roughly 36 percent by the river. The true figures are 19.6 percent with one card left and 35 percent with two. The shortcut works because each unseen card is about 2 percent of the deck you cannot see.
The numbers worth knowing cold

Four outs, a gutshot: about 9 percent on one card and 16.5 percent with two. Six outs, two overcards hoping to pair: about 13 and 24 percent. Eight outs, the open-ended straight draw: about 17 and 31.5 percent. Nine outs, the flush draw: about 19.6 and 35 percent. Fifteen outs, a straight and flush draw combined: about 33 percent on one card and 54 percent with two. That last hand is a favourite over a made pair, which surprises many players the first time they see it.
Fix the shortcut for big draws

The rule of four overstates large draws. Fifteen outs times four is 60, but the real figure is 54 percent. The correction is simple: when you have more than eight outs, take the number of outs above eight and subtract it from your answer. Fifteen is seven more than eight, and 60 minus 7 is 53, within a point of the truth. For draws of eight outs or fewer the plain rule is accurate enough that no fix is needed.
Not every out is clean

Some cards that complete your hand also complete a better one for someone else. If you hold a straight draw on a board with two spades, the two cards that make your straight in spades may hand an opponent a flush. If you hope to pair your ace against someone holding ace king, that pair leaves you second best. Experienced players discount tainted outs, counting a doubtful card as half an out or none. Overcounting outs is the most common way a draw gets overvalued.
Use four only when you see both cards

The rule of four assumes you will see the turn and the river for the price you pay now. That is only true if you or your opponent is all in on the flop. If there is more betting to come, your opponent can charge you again on the turn, and you should compare the bet in front of you with your chance on the next card alone, the rule of two. Using four on the flop when another bet is coming is how players talk themselves into bad calls.
Put it together with the price

The method is two numbers side by side. Count your clean outs and convert them to a percentage. Work out the percentage the pot is asking for. If the first is bigger, continue. If it is smaller, fold, unless you expect to win a lot more when you hit. With practice the whole comparison takes two or three seconds. It replaces the vague sense that a draw is promising with a figure, and the figure is right far more often than the feeling.
Power is volts times amps

Power, measured in watts, is how fast energy is being used. In a circuit it is voltage multiplied by current. A phone charger delivering 5 volts at 2 amps supplies 10 watts. A 12 volt car headlamp drawing 5 amps uses 60 watts. Substituting Ohm's law gives two more forms: current squared times resistance, and voltage squared divided by resistance. All three give the same answer. Pick whichever uses the two numbers you already know, and you can find the power in any part of a circuit.
Every part has a limit

A resistor does not just have a resistance. It has a power rating, the heat it can shed without cooking. The common small through-hole resistor is rated a quarter of a watt. Put 5 volts across a 100 ohm one and it dissipates 25 divided by 100, a quarter of a watt, right at its limit and too hot to touch. Put 12 volts across it and it must shed 1.44 watts. It will brown, smell and fail. The value was right. The size was wrong.
Why the square matters

Because power rises with the square of current, small increases hurt more than you expect. Double the current through a wire and it makes four times the heat. Triple it and you get nine times. This is why an extension cord that runs a lamp happily gets dangerously warm feeding a space heater, and why power companies send electricity long distances at very high voltage. For the same power, higher voltage means lower current, and lower current means far less energy wasted heating the wires along the way.
Leave yourself a margin

Good practice is to run parts at no more than about half their rating. If a resistor will dissipate 0.2 watts, use a half watt part. The same thinking applies to capacitors and voltage, to transistors and current, and to power supplies. A part run at its limit works on the bench and fails in a closed box on a hot day, because ratings assume air at room temperature moving freely. Derating, as engineers call it, is the cheapest reliability you can buy.
Getting the heat out

When a part must handle real power, the design job becomes moving heat away. That is what the finned metal heatsinks on amplifiers and voltage regulators do. They give the heat more surface to leave from. A fan helps further by replacing the warm air. Thermal paste fills the microscopic gaps between a chip and its heatsink, because air is a poor conductor of heat. A regulator that shuts down after ten minutes is usually not broken. It is hot, and it is protecting itself.
Batteries are a power budget

Power thinking also tells you how long a battery lasts. A battery's capacity is given in amp hours or milliamp hours, the current it can supply multiplied by the time. A 2,000 milliamp hour cell feeding a circuit that draws 100 milliamps lasts roughly 20 hours. Multiply capacity by voltage and you get watt hours, the honest measure of stored energy and the number airlines use to limit what you can carry on. If a gadget dies early, measure what it draws while asleep. A forgotten 5 milliamps runs all day, every day.
The check to run

For any part that feels warm, work out the power. Measure the voltage across it and the current through it, multiply, and compare with the rating on the datasheet. If you are above half, change something: a larger part, a higher resistance, a lower voltage or a heatsink. Smell is also a tool. Overheated resistors and circuit boards have a sharp, sweet, burnt odour that people who repair electronics learn to recognize from across a room. If you smell it, cut the power first and investigate second.
A share, not a verdict

Equity is the percentage of the time your hand will win if all the remaining cards are dealt with no more betting. If you would win 60 times in 100, you have 60 percent equity, and 60 percent of the pot is yours in the long-run sense. On any single deal you win everything or nothing. Over thousands of deals the results converge on the share. Thinking this way separates the quality of a decision from the luck of one outcome.
The match-ups to memorize

A few preflop confrontations come up constantly. A higher pair against a lower pair, such as aces against kings, is roughly an 80 to 20 favourite. A pair against two higher cards, queens against ace king, is close to even, about 55 to 45 for the pair. That is the classic coin flip. A hand that shares a card with a better kicker, ace king against ace queen, is about a 70 to 30 favourite. Two higher cards against two lower ones, ace king against 7 6, is only around 60 to 40.
Nothing is ever dead before the flop

The striking thing about those numbers is how much the weaker hand keeps. The worst common match-up, an underpair against an overpair, still wins about one time in five. Seven two offsuit, the worst starting hand, wins roughly one time in nine against a pair of aces. This is why all-in pots before the flop swing so wildly and why a single lost coin flip tells you nothing about how you played. The cards to come carry a great deal of the result.
Equity moves with every card

Your share is recalculated each time a card lands. Ace king against a pair of queens starts at about 45 percent. If the flop comes without an ace or a king, it falls to roughly 24 percent, because you now have six outs and two cards to come. If an ace lands, the positions reverse and the queens are left with two outs, around 8 percent. Strong players track this as the board develops. The hand you started with matters less on each street than the share you hold now.
Betting is about denying or charging

Once you think in shares, the reason to bet with a good hand becomes clear. An opponent with a flush draw owns about a third of the pot on the flop. If you check and let them see cards for free, they collect that share at no cost. If you bet, they must either pay more than their share is worth or fold and surrender it. Giving free cards to hands with real equity is one of the quietest ways to lose money.
Equity against a range

You never know your opponent's exact cards, so real equity is measured against the whole set of hands they could hold. Against someone who only raises with aces, kings, queens and ace king, a pair of jacks has only about 36 percent. Against someone raising a wide assortment of hands, the same jacks may have 65 percent. The cards have not changed. The opponent has. That is why the same hand can be a fold against one player and a confident raise against another.
Practise away from the table

Free equity calculators let you enter two hands, or a hand against a range, and see the shares. Spending twenty minutes entering the situations you were unsure about is the fastest way to build intuition. After a few weeks you stop guessing. You simply know that a pair plus a flush draw is around 50 percent against top pair, that two overcards and a gutshot have about 40 percent, and that a bare gutshot is seldom worth chasing.
One path or several

Parts are in series when they sit end to end on a single path, so the same current has to pass through each in turn. Parts are in parallel when they connect across the same two points, so each gets the same voltage and the current splits between them. Old strings of holiday lights were wired in series, which is why one dead bulb darkened the lot. The sockets in your house are wired in parallel, which is why switching off a lamp does not switch off the refrigerator.
Series: resistance adds, voltage divides

In series, resistances add. A 100 ohm and a 220 ohm resistor in series behave as 320 ohms. The same current flows through both, and the supply voltage is shared between them in proportion to their values, with the bigger resistor taking the bigger share. On a 3.2 volt supply, that pair would pass 10 milliamps, with 1 volt across the first and 2.2 across the second. The shares always add up to the supply. That bookkeeping rule is called Kirchhoff's voltage law.
Parallel: more paths, less resistance

In parallel, adding a resistor always lowers the total resistance, because you have opened another path. Two equal resistors in parallel make half of one. Two 1 kilohm resistors give 500 ohms. For unequal values, multiply the two and divide by their sum. A 1 kilohm and a 3 kilohm pair gives 750 ohms. The total is always smaller than the smallest branch. Each branch draws its own current as if the others were not there, and the supply must provide the sum.
Batteries follow the same logic

Cells in series add their voltages. Four 1.5 volt AA cells end to end make 6 volts, with the same capacity as one cell. Cells in parallel keep the voltage of one but add their capacities, so the pack lasts longer or delivers more current. Laptop and electric car packs combine both, with groups of parallel cells stacked in series. Mixing old and new cells is a bad idea in either arrangement, because the weaker cell gets driven by the stronger ones, heats up and can leak.
Why overloaded outlets trip

Every appliance plugged into a household circuit is in parallel with the others. Each one adds its current to the total flowing through the wire in the wall. A kettle and a toaster together can draw more than the wire is rated to carry. The circuit breaker exists to notice that total and open the loop before the wire overheats. So a tripped breaker is not a fault in any one appliance. It is the sum of the parallel branches exceeding what the shared wire can safely handle.
Capacitors do the opposite

Resistors add in series and shrink in parallel. Capacitors do the reverse. Two capacitors in parallel simply add, because you have made a bigger tank. Two in series give less than either one, using the same multiply and divide by the sum rule that parallel resistors use. That is why you often see several small capacitors side by side on a board: together they act as one larger part, and they respond faster than a single big one would. Knowing which rule belongs to which part saves a lot of confusion later.
Reading a real circuit

Real circuits mix both arrangements, and the skill is spotting which is which. Follow a wire from one part. If the only place the current can go next is into a second part, those two are in series. If the two parts share both ends, they are in parallel. Collapse each simple group into a single equivalent value, redraw, and repeat. A tangle of a dozen resistors usually reduces to one number in a few steps. This is the first technique taught in every circuits course, and working engineers never stop using it.
The average result of a decision

Expected value, EV for short, is what a decision earns on average if you could repeat it thousands of times. To find it, multiply each possible outcome by its chance and add them up. Suppose you call 50 dollars to win a pot of 150, and you will win 30 percent of the time. You win 150 three times in ten and lose 50 seven times in ten. That is 45 minus 35, a profit of 10 dollars per call on average. The call is plus EV, even though you lose most of the time.
Good decisions can lose

In the example above you lose the pot seven times out of ten and the call is still correct. A player who judges by results will decide after a few losses that the call was a mistake and stop making it. That player has just made their game worse. The reverse is equally common. Someone calls with a hopeless hand, hits a miracle card and concludes the play works. Short-term results in poker are loud and mostly noise. EV is the quiet signal beneath them.
Every option has an EV

At each decision you are comparing options, not judging one. Folding has an EV of exactly zero from that point: you win nothing and lose nothing more. Money already in the pot is gone and does not count. Calling has some EV. Raising has another. The right play is whichever is highest, and sometimes the best available option is still negative, in which case folding at zero wins. Treating chips already invested as a reason to continue is the sunk cost mistake in its purest form.
Small edges, many times

A single plus EV decision may be worth a dollar or two. That seems trivial until you count how many decisions a regular player makes. Several hundred hands in a live week, tens of thousands a month online. A consistent edge of a fraction of a bet per hand is the whole of a winning player's income. Casinos work the same way with an edge of a few percent on each wager. Nobody gets rich on one hand. They get rich on the same small advantage, repeated without boredom.
The EV of a bluff

A bluff has two outcomes. Either the opponent folds and you win the pot, or they call and you usually lose your bet. Bet 50 into a pot of 100 with nothing. If they fold 40 percent of the time, you win 100 four times in ten and lose 50 six times in ten: 40 minus 30, a profit of 10 dollars. The break-even point for a half-pot bluff is one fold in three. Bluffing is not courage. It is a calculation about how often the other person lets go.
Estimate, do not compute

Nobody runs exact sums at the table. What strong players do is estimate the two or three numbers that matter, then lean the right way. Is this call roughly break-even, clearly good or clearly bad? Will this opponent fold more than a third of the time? Rough answers to the right questions beat precise answers to the wrong ones. The precision comes later, in review, when you can check the hard spots with a calculator and correct your instincts for next time.
Why it protects your mind

EV thinking is also armour. When you know a decision was correct, a bad result stings less, because you understand that you would make the same play again and profit in the long run. Players who lack this frame take every lost pot as evidence of bad luck or personal failure and start playing worse, a slide known as tilt. Keeping score by the quality of decisions, not by the size of tonight's stack, is how professionals stay level through the swings.
Two resistors in a row

Connect two resistors in series across a supply and tap the point where they meet. The voltage at that point is a fixed fraction of the supply. With equal resistors it is exactly half. In general, it is the supply voltage times the bottom resistor divided by the sum of both. A 10 kilohm resistor on top and a 20 kilohm on the bottom across 9 volts gives 6 volts at the middle. Nothing else is involved. The ratio of the two parts sets the output, whatever their absolute values.
Turning resistance into voltage

Many sensors work by changing resistance. A thermistor changes with temperature, a photocell with light, a flex sensor with bending. A microcontroller cannot measure resistance directly. It measures voltage. So you pair the sensor with a fixed resistor to make a divider, and the midpoint voltage now moves as the sensor's resistance moves. The humble divider is the translator between the physical world and the input pin. If you ever wire a light sensor to an Arduino, this is the circuit you are building.
A volume knob is a divider

A potentiometer is a strip of resistive material with a sliding contact. The two ends go across the signal and the slider picks off a fraction of it. Turning the knob changes the ratio of the resistance above the slider to the resistance below it. That is a voltage divider you adjust by hand. Volume controls, light dimmer inputs, joysticks and the position sensors in older throttle pedals all work this way. One part gives you every ratio from zero to one.
Stepping signals down safely

Dividers also shrink voltages to levels a chip can accept. A 5 volt sensor output feeding a 3.3 volt input pin can pass through a 10 kilohm and 20 kilohm divider and arrive at 3.3 volts. A 12 volt battery can be measured by a chip that tolerates only 3.3 volts by dividing by four or more first. The chip reads the smaller number and the software multiplies it back up. This is how nearly every battery gauge senses its own pack voltage.
The catch: loading

A divider only holds its ratio if almost no current is drawn from the midpoint. Whatever you connect there is effectively in parallel with the bottom resistor, which changes the ratio. Feed a motor from a divider and the voltage collapses. The rule of thumb is that the load should have at least ten times the resistance of the divider's resistors. That is why a divider is fine for signals and references, and why you never use one to power anything. Power needs a regulator, which adjusts itself as the load changes.
Dividers you did not mean to build

Dividers also appear by accident. A corroded connector adds a few ohms in series with a load, and the supply voltage is now shared between the corrosion and the load. The load sees less than it should, and the bad connection gets warm. A weak battery behaves the same way: its internal resistance rises with age, so it measures fine with nothing attached and sags the moment a motor asks for current. Mechanics chase this fault constantly. Measuring the voltage at the load while it is running, not at the battery while idle, exposes it.
Choosing the values

Small resistors make a stiff divider that tolerates loading but wastes current all day. Large ones save power but become sensitive to loading and electrical noise. For signals into a microcontroller, values between 1 kilohm and 100 kilohms are the usual range, with 10 kilohms the common default. In battery gadgets designers push toward hundreds of kilohms to save every microamp. When you see two resistors in series with a wire leaving from between them on a schematic, you now know what you are looking at.
Looking past the current bet

Pot odds measure the money in the middle now. Implied odds add the money you expect to win on later streets if you make your hand. Suppose you face a bet of 20 into 40 with a draw that hits about 18 percent of the time. You need 25 percent, so the call looks wrong. But if your opponent will pay you another 100 when you hit, you are really risking 20 to win 160. That needs only about 11 percent, and the call becomes clearly profitable.
Set mining is the classic case

Small and medium pocket pairs are the textbook example. You will flop three of a kind or better about 12 percent of the time, roughly one flop in eight and a half. The immediate pot odds before the flop almost never justify a call on that basis. The call makes sense because a flopped set is well hidden and often wins a very large pot. A common guideline is that you and your opponent should each have at least 15 to 20 times the size of the call behind for the play to pay.
Stack depth decides everything

Implied odds are limited by the smaller stack in the hand. If your opponent has only 60 dollars left and you must call 20, the most you can win later is 60, however perfectly you hit. This is why speculative hands such as small pairs and suited connectors gain value when stacks are deep and lose it when stacks are short. In a tournament with ten big blinds, those hands are nearly worthless. With 200 big blinds in a cash game, they are among the most profitable.
Hidden hands get paid, obvious ones do not

The value of hitting depends on whether your opponent can see it coming. A set is disguised, since nobody can tell from the board that you hold a pair in your hand. A straight made with connected cards is often disguised too. A flush is the opposite. When the third card of a suit lands, everyone notices, and a careful opponent slows down. So flush draws have weaker implied odds than players assume, and a draw to anything but the highest flush can cost you money when a bigger one is out.
The opponent matters most

Implied odds are a prediction about another person. Against a player who cannot fold top pair, they are enormous. Against a cautious player who gives up the moment the board turns frightening, they barely exist. Before making a call that depends on future winnings, ask what this particular opponent does with a good but second best hand. If the answer is that they keep betting or keep calling, call. If they shut down, you are paying full price for a prize you will not collect.
Reverse implied odds

The idea also runs backwards. Some hands tend to win small pots and lose big ones. Hold king jack on a king high flop and you will often win a little when you are ahead and lose a lot when someone holds ace king or king queen. A weak flush draw has the same problem when it gets there against a bigger flush. These are reverse implied odds: the money you expect to lose later when your hand improves to second best. Dominated hands are the main culprits.
An honest test

Implied odds are the most abused concept in poker, because they can excuse any call. To keep yourself honest, state the amount out loud: how much more must I win, on average, when I hit, for this call to break even? Then ask whether this opponent, with these stacks, on this kind of board, will really pay that. If you cannot say yes with a straight face, the call is not about implied odds. It is about wanting to see another card.
Two kinds of flow

Direct current, DC, flows in one direction, like water down a river. Batteries, solar panels and USB ports supply DC. Alternating current, AC, flows back and forth, reversing direction on a regular beat. The power from a wall socket is AC. In North America it completes 60 full cycles a second and in most of the rest of the world it completes 50. Nearly all electronics run on DC inside, which is why almost everything you plug in begins by converting one into the other.
Why the grid chose AC

In the 1880s, Thomas Edison's DC systems and the AC systems backed by George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla competed to electrify cities. AC won for one practical reason: the transformer. A transformer changes AC voltage up or down with nothing but two coils of wire around an iron core. That let power stations send electricity at high voltage, where little is lost in the wires, and step it down near homes. DC had no equally simple way to change voltage at the time, so DC stations had to sit within a mile or so of their customers.
What the wall numbers mean

A North American socket is called 120 volts, but the voltage is a smooth wave that swings to about plus 170 volts and back to minus 170. The 120 figure is the RMS value, the steady DC voltage that would deliver the same heating power. Most of Europe, Asia and Africa use about 230 volts RMS. Higher voltage means less current for the same power, which is why a kettle in Britain boils noticeably faster than one in the United States on an ordinary socket.
Turning AC into DC

A power adapter does the conversion in stages. A transformer or switching stage brings the voltage down. Diodes, which pass current in one direction only, flip the negative half of the wave so that it all points the same way. That step is called rectifying. A large capacitor then fills in the gaps between the bumps, and a regulator trims the result to a steady figure such as 5 volts. Old adapters were heavy because they used iron transformers. Modern ones are small because they switch at high frequency, which needs far less iron.
DC is making a comeback

The grid is AC, but more and more of what connects to it is DC by nature. Solar panels make DC. Batteries store DC. LEDs, computers and electric car motors' controllers run on DC. Modern power electronics can now change DC voltages efficiently, the thing Edison lacked. That is why very long transmission links increasingly use high voltage DC, and why USB has quietly become a household DC standard, delivering up to 240 watts in its latest version, enough for a laptop or a monitor.
Frequency and why plugs differ

The number of cycles a second is called frequency and is measured in hertz. Clocks and motors once relied on it for timing, which is one reason an appliance built for one country may misbehave in another even with a plug adapter. Voltage is the bigger hazard. A 120 volt hair dryer on a 230 volt socket draws about four times its rated power for a moment and then fails, sometimes dramatically. Most phone and laptop chargers are marked 100 to 240 volts and work anywhere. Read the small print on the label before you travel.
What matters at the bench

Three practical points follow. First, polarity matters on DC: connect a part backwards and it may be destroyed, so check the plus and minus marks. Second, mains AC is dangerous in a way small DC supplies are not. Work on the low voltage side of an adapter and leave the wall side closed unless you are trained. Third, when a multimeter reads nonsense, check its dial. Measuring a battery on the AC setting or a socket on the DC setting produces numbers that look almost plausible and mean nothing.
Two ways to win

When you check or call, you can only win by showing down the best hand. When you bet or raise, you add a second path: your opponent may fold. Fold equity is the value of that second path, the share of the pot you pick up simply because the other player gives in. It is the reason aggressive poker beats passive poker over time. The passive player needs the best cards. The aggressive player needs either the best cards or an opponent who is not willing to continue.
How often a bluff must work

The arithmetic for a pure bluff is short. Divide your bet by the total of the pot plus your bet. A bet of half the pot must succeed one time in three. A bet of two thirds of the pot must work 40 percent of the time. A pot-sized bet needs to work half the time. A bet of one third of the pot needs only one fold in four. Smaller bluffs need to work less often but are easier to call, so the two effects pull against each other.
The semi-bluff adds a third way

A semi-bluff is a bet with a hand that is probably behind now but can improve, such as a flush draw. It wins if the opponent folds, and it can still win if they call and you hit. Take a pot of 100 and a bet of 100. If the opponent folds 40 percent of the time and you have 35 percent equity when called, the play earns about 43 dollars on average. With no equity at all, the same bet would lose 20. The draw turns a losing bluff into a strong play.
Who you bet into matters

Fold equity is a property of the opponent, not of your cards. Some players call far too much and almost never fold a pair. Against them your fold equity is close to zero, and bluffing is setting money on fire. Others fold too readily when the bet is large or the board is frightening. Against them, hands with no showdown value at all become profitable bets. The first adjustment a thinking player makes at any table is deciding which kind of opponent is in each seat.
Your image and your story

People fold when the bet is believable. A player who has been caught bluffing twice in the last hour has little fold equity for a while. One who has shown down only strong hands has plenty. The line you take in the hand matters too. A bluff is credible when your earlier actions fit the strong hand you are now representing. A sudden large bet on the river from someone who checked every street before it tells a story that does not add up, and observant opponents call it.
Short stacks lose it

Fold equity shrinks as your stack does. A raise only frightens someone if it puts meaningful chips at risk. In a tournament, a player with fifteen big blinds who moves all in can still force folds from hands that do not want to gamble. A player with four big blinds cannot, because calling costs so little that almost any hand is priced in. This is why waiting too long to make a move with a dwindling stack is a mistake: you give up the weapon before you use it.
The takeaway

Every time you consider betting, estimate two numbers. How often does this opponent fold to this bet? How much equity do I have when they do not? If the folds alone make the bet profitable, your cards hardly matter. If they do not, you need real equity to make up the difference. Players who only bet when they have a hand are easy to read and easy to beat. Players who understand fold equity win pots that their cards alone never would.
What a resistor is for

A resistor does one thing: it resists current by a known amount. That single ability covers a surprising range of jobs. It limits the current into an LED so the LED survives. It sets the gain of an amplifier. It holds an unused input pin at a definite level. It turns a current into a voltage so that a chip can measure it. A typical circuit board carries more resistors than any other part. They cost a fraction of a cent each in quantity, which is why designers reach for one whenever a current needs taming.
Reading the colour bands

Through-hole resistors carry coloured bands because numbers would be too small to print. The colours stand for digits: black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, grey 8, white 9. On a four band part, the first two bands are digits and the third is the number of zeros to add. Yellow, violet, red reads 4, 7 and two zeros: 4,700 ohms, or 4.7 kilohms. The last band, set slightly apart, gives the tolerance. Gold means 5 percent, brown 1 percent.
Surface mount codes

The tiny rectangular resistors on modern boards use printed numbers. A three digit code works like the bands: two digits and a count of zeros. So 103 means 10 followed by three zeros, 10,000 ohms. 472 is 4,700 ohms. The letter R marks a decimal point, so 4R7 is 4.7 ohms. A part marked 0 or 000 is a zero ohm link, a resistor shaped wire that lets a machine place a jumper. The smallest sizes carry no marking at all, and the only way to identify one is to measure it.
Why the values look odd

Resistors come in values such as 10, 22, 33, 47 and 68, repeated at every power of ten. The numbers look arbitrary but are spaced so that each is roughly the same percentage above the last. With 5 percent parts, the ranges of neighbouring values just touch, so every possible resistance is covered by something on the shelf. The standard set is called the E series. You rarely need an exact value. Pick the nearest standard one, and if precision matters, pick a tighter tolerance.
Tolerance and what it costs

A 5 percent, 1 kilohm resistor may really be anywhere from 950 to 1,050 ohms. For limiting LED current or pulling a pin high, that is irrelevant. For a voltage divider that sets a measurement, it matters, because the error passes straight into the reading. One percent parts cost almost nothing extra today and are the sensible default. Precision references and instrument inputs use 0.1 percent parts that also drift very little as they warm up. Buy accuracy only where the circuit's result depends on it.
The power rating is the other number

Size tells you how much heat a resistor can shed. The common through-hole part handles a quarter of a watt. The tiny surface mount ones handle a tenth or less. Work out the power with voltage squared divided by resistance and stay under half the rating. A resistor asked to dissipate too much does not fail politely. It discolours, drifts upward in value, and eventually cracks or chars the board beneath it. If you find a scorched patch on an old circuit board, there was usually a hard working resistor above it.
Three mistakes to skip

First, measuring a resistor while it is still in a powered circuit, which gives nonsense and can damage the meter. Power off first. Second, measuring it in circuit and trusting the number: other parts in parallel pull the reading down, so lift one leg if it matters. Third, holding both leads with your fingers on a high value part. Your skin is a resistor of a few hundred kilohms to a few megohms, and it is now in parallel with the thing you are trying to measure.
Two plates and a gap

A capacitor is two conductors separated by an insulator. Push charge onto one plate and an equal charge is repelled from the other, and energy is stored in the electric field between them. The amount it can hold per volt is its capacitance, measured in farads. A farad is enormous, so real parts are rated in microfarads, nanofarads and picofarads, each a thousand times smaller than the last. Unlike a battery, a capacitor stores very little, but it can take in or give out that energy almost instantly.
It resists changes in voltage

The useful way to think of a capacitor is that it hates a sudden change in the voltage across it. To change that voltage, charge must flow in or out, and that takes time. So a capacitor across a power supply fills the dips and absorbs the spikes, like a small reservoir on a water main. This is the most common use of all. Every digital chip has one or more small capacitors right next to its power pins for this reason, and removing them makes otherwise good circuits behave unpredictably.
It passes AC and blocks DC

Apply a steady voltage and a capacitor charges up, then no more current flows. Apply a changing voltage and current keeps flowing in and out as the plates charge and discharge. So a capacitor in series with a signal lets the wiggle through while stopping any steady level underneath it. Audio equipment uses this to pass music between stages that sit at different DC voltages. The higher the frequency, the more easily it passes, which is also why capacitors are the basic ingredient of filters.
Timing with a resistor

A capacitor charged through a resistor takes a predictable time to fill. Multiply the resistance in ohms by the capacitance in farads and you get the time constant in seconds, the time to reach about 63 percent of the supply. Ten kilohms and 100 microfarads gives one second. After five time constants the capacitor is essentially full. This simple pair sets delays, blink rates and the cut-off points of filters. The intermittent setting on windscreen wipers was first built from exactly this arrangement.
The main types

Ceramic capacitors are small, cheap and not polarized, and they cover the range from picofarads to a few tens of microfarads. Electrolytic capacitors pack far more capacitance into a can, hundreds or thousands of microfarads, but they are polarized: one lead must stay more positive than the other. Film capacitors are stable and favoured in audio and mains circuits. Supercapacitors reach whole farads and can run a small circuit for minutes or hours. The type matters as much as the value, so read both before substituting one for another.
Polarity and voltage ratings

An electrolytic capacitor connected backwards, or run above its voltage rating, can fail violently. The can is scored on top so that it splits open instead of bursting. The stripe on the side marks the negative lead. Always pick a voltage rating comfortably above what the circuit applies, usually by half again or more. Old electrolytics dry out with heat and age, and bulging tops on the capacitors near a power supply are one of the most common causes of dead monitors, routers and motherboards.
Respect a charged capacitor

A capacitor holds its charge after the power is removed. Small ones are harmless. Large ones in power supplies, camera flashes, microwave ovens and tube amplifiers can hold a dangerous charge for minutes or longer. Technicians discharge them through a resistor before touching anything and then measure to confirm. Shorting one with a screwdriver works but makes a loud bang and pits the tool. If a device plugs into the wall and you are not sure what is inside, assume the big capacitors are charged until a meter says otherwise.
A coil with a memory

Any current creates a magnetic field around its wire. Wind the wire into a coil and the fields of the turns add together. Building that field takes energy, and collapsing it gives the energy back. The result is a part that resists changes in current the way a heavy flywheel resists changes in speed. Its strength is called inductance, measured in henries, with real parts usually in microhenries or millihenries. Adding an iron or ferrite core concentrates the field and multiplies the inductance many times over.
The mirror image of a capacitor

A capacitor resists changes in voltage and passes fast signals easily. An inductor resists changes in current and passes steady current easily while opposing fast changes. Put simply, capacitors block DC and inductors block high frequencies. Used together they make filters that select or reject a band of frequencies. An old radio tuning dial moved the plates of a capacitor against a fixed coil to choose a station. The same pairing is still inside every radio, phone and wireless charger made today.
Kickback

Because an inductor insists that its current keep flowing, interrupting that current abruptly has a dramatic effect. The collapsing field generates whatever voltage it needs to keep the current going, often hundreds of volts from a 12 volt circuit. This is how a car's ignition coil makes a spark. It is also how a relay or motor destroys the transistor that switches it. The cure is a diode placed backwards across the coil, called a flyback diode, which gives the current a harmless loop to die away in.
How switching supplies use it

The inductor's stubbornness is what makes efficient power conversion possible. A switching regulator connects an inductor to the supply for a moment, storing energy in its field, then disconnects it and lets the inductor deliver that energy to the output. Doing this hundreds of thousands of times a second, and varying how long the switch stays on, produces a lower or higher voltage with very little wasted as heat. Phone chargers, laptop adapters and the converters on every motherboard work this way.
Transformers are two inductors sharing a field

Wind two coils on the same core and a changing current in the first induces a voltage in the second. The ratio of the turns sets the ratio of the voltages. Ten times the turns on the output gives ten times the voltage and a tenth of the current. Because only a changing field induces anything, transformers work on AC and not on steady DC. They also isolate: no wire connects the input to the output, which is what makes a mains adapter safe to touch on its low voltage side.
Ferrite beads and chokes

An inductor used simply to block unwanted high frequency noise is called a choke. The lump moulded onto many laptop and monitor cables is a ferrite sleeve doing this job, soaking up radio frequency interference travelling along the wire. On circuit boards, tiny ferrite beads sit in series with power lines to keep the noise of one section out of another. They cost almost nothing and are often the difference between a product that passes its radio emissions test and one that fails it.
Reading an inductor's limits

Two ratings matter beyond the inductance. The saturation current is the point at which the core cannot hold any more magnetic field. Past it the inductance collapses and the current shoots up, a common cause of failed power converters. The resistance of the winding is the other, since it wastes power as heat. A physically larger inductor of the same value generally has a higher saturation current and lower resistance. When a design calls for a specific inductor, substitute by all three numbers, never by inductance alone.
A check valve for electrons

A diode has two leads, the anode and the cathode. Current flows easily from anode to cathode and hardly at all the other way. On the part, a stripe marks the cathode end. On a schematic, the symbol is an arrow pointing at a bar, and the arrow shows the direction current is allowed to flow. Inside is a junction between two differently treated regions of silicon. The junction is the foundation of nearly all semiconductor devices, and a diode is the simplest thing you can build from one.
The forward drop

A diode is not a perfect valve. It needs a small voltage to open, and it keeps roughly that much for itself while conducting. For an ordinary silicon diode the figure is about 0.6 to 0.7 volts. Below it almost nothing flows. Above it the current rises steeply. That lost voltage becomes heat: a diode carrying 3 amps with 0.7 volts across it dissipates about 2 watts. Schottky diodes use a metal junction instead and drop only 0.2 to 0.4 volts, which is why they appear wherever efficiency matters.
Rectifying AC

The classic job is turning AC into DC. One diode passes only the positive half of the wave. Four diodes arranged in a diamond, called a bridge rectifier, steer both halves so they emerge pointing the same way. Follow that with a capacitor and you have rough DC. Every device that plugs into a wall contains this arrangement somewhere near its input. Bridge rectifiers are sold as single four-legged blocks marked with a wave symbol on two legs and plus and minus on the others.
Protecting against mistakes

A diode in series with a power input stops damage if the battery or adapter is connected backwards, at the cost of its forward drop. A diode across a relay coil absorbs the voltage spike when the coil is switched off. Two diodes from an input pin to the supply rails clamp any spike to a safe level, and most chips have these built in. Protection is unglamorous, but it is the reason modern gadgets survive static shocks and reversed plugs that would have destroyed electronics of fifty years ago.
Zener diodes work backwards on purpose

Every diode breaks down and conducts if enough reverse voltage is applied. A Zener diode is built so that this happens at a precise, repeatable voltage, such as 5.1 or 12 volts, without harming it. Wired in reverse with a resistor in series, it holds a steady voltage across itself while the input varies. It makes a simple voltage reference or a clamp that keeps a line from rising too high. For precision, a dedicated reference chip is better, but a Zener is cheap and nearly indestructible.
Light in, light out

Some diodes are built to interact with light. An LED emits light when current flows forward through it, with the colour set by the material. A photodiode does the reverse, producing a small current when light falls on it, and is the sensor in remote control receivers, smoke detectors and fibre optic links. A solar cell is a very large photodiode arranged to deliver power. All three are the same junction, optimized for a different job.
Testing a diode

Most multimeters have a diode setting, marked with the diode symbol. It pushes a small current through the part and shows the forward voltage. A good silicon diode reads about 0.5 to 0.7 one way and shows open circuit the other way. A reading near zero both ways means it has failed short. Open both ways means it has failed open. The same test checks the junctions inside a transistor, and with an LED it usually makes the part glow faintly, which conveniently tells you which lead is which.
A diode that glows

A light emitting diode is a diode made from materials that release light when current crosses the junction. The colour depends on the material, not on any coating. Red and green LEDs appeared in the 1960s and 70s. An efficient blue one arrived only in the early 1990s, work that earned Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics. Blue made white light possible, by coating a blue LED with a phosphor that converts part of its output to yellow.
Voltage is set by colour

Each colour has its own forward voltage. Red runs at about 1.8 to 2.2 volts. Yellow and older green are similar. Blue, white and modern bright green need about 3 to 3.3 volts. This is a property of the part, and you cannot change it. It means a 3 volt coin cell lights a red LED easily and a blue one only barely, and that a red and a blue LED wired directly in parallel will not share: the red one takes nearly all the current.
Why it needs a resistor

Once an LED reaches its forward voltage, a tiny further increase in voltage produces a huge increase in current. Connect one straight to a supply and nothing limits that current except the supply itself. The LED overheats and fails in a fraction of a second, sometimes with a pop. A series resistor absorbs the difference between the supply and the forward voltage and so fixes the current. Subtract the LED's voltage from the supply, divide by the current you want, and you have the value.
How much current to give it

A standard indicator LED is rated for 20 milliamps, but modern ones are so efficient that 1 to 5 milliamps is plenty for a status light indoors. Running at a fraction of the rating saves power and extends life. High power LEDs for lighting are a different animal, running at 350 milliamps to several amps. Those need a constant current driver circuit and a heatsink. A resistor would waste too much power and would not hold the current steady as the LED warms up.
Which leg is which

An LED only lights one way round. On a new through-hole part the longer leg is the anode, the positive side. The plastic rim usually has a flat spot beside the cathode, the negative side. Inside the lens, the larger metal piece is generally the cathode. Surface mount LEDs carry a green mark or a notch at the cathode end. Connecting an ordinary LED backwards at low voltage does not hurt it. It simply stays dark, which makes reversed polarity the first thing to check.
Dimming without changing colour

Lowering the current dims an LED, but the colour of white LEDs shifts slightly as it drops. The preferred method is to switch the LED fully on and fully off very fast and vary the fraction of time it is on. Above a few hundred times a second the eye sees a steady, dimmer light. The technique is called pulse width modulation. Poorly designed dimmers switch too slowly, which is the flicker some people notice in cheap bulbs and car tail lights when their eyes move.
What actually kills them

LEDs do not burn out like filaments. They fade, and heat is the cause. An LED's rated life, often 25,000 hours or more, is the time until its output falls to 70 percent, assuming it is kept cool. In a household bulb the LEDs themselves usually outlast the cramped, hot driver electronics packed in the base. That is why a bulb in an enclosed fixture fails early, and why the first sign of death is often flickering instead of darkness.
Three legs, one job

A bipolar junction transistor has three terminals: base, collector and emitter. A small current flowing into the base allows a much larger current to flow from collector to emitter. With no base current, the path is closed. The ratio between the two currents is the gain, typically 100 or more for a small transistor. So a microcontroller pin that can supply only a few milliamps can, through a transistor, control a motor, a relay or a strip of lights drawing a hundred times as much.
NPN and PNP

Transistors come in two polarities. An NPN transistor turns on when its base is driven positive relative to its emitter and is used to switch the ground side of a load. A PNP transistor is the mirror image, turning on when its base is pulled below its emitter, and switches the positive side. Beginners should start with NPN, since it matches the way logic outputs work: pin high, load on. The common 2N3904 and its cousin the 2N2222 are NPN parts that have been in production for more than half a century.
The standard switch circuit

Connect the load between the positive supply and the collector. Connect the emitter to ground. Connect the control pin to the base through a resistor. When the pin goes high, current flows through the resistor into the base, the transistor conducts and the load turns on. The resistor is essential. The base behaves like a diode to ground, and without a resistor the pin would try to supply unlimited current into it. A value of 1 kilohm suits most small loads driven from 5 volts.
Saturation: fully on

For switching, you want the transistor fully on, a state called saturation, where the voltage left across it is only about 0.2 volts. To guarantee that, supply noticeably more base current than the gain calculation strictly requires. A common rule is to assume a gain of only 10 or 20. For a 100 milliamp load, that means 5 to 10 milliamps into the base. A transistor that is only partly on drops several volts while carrying current, so it runs hot and may fail.
Protecting it from the load

Loads with coils, such as relays, motors and solenoids, kick back with a high voltage spike when switched off. Place a diode across the load with its stripe toward the positive supply and the spike circulates harmlessly. Leave it out and the transistor may work for days before failing, which makes the fault hard to connect to its cause. This diode is the most often forgotten part in beginner circuits, and adding it costs a couple of cents.
When to use something else

A small bipolar transistor is right for loads up to a few hundred milliamps. Beyond that, the base current needed becomes awkward and the 0.2 volt drop starts to waste real power. The usual step up is a MOSFET, which is controlled by voltage and wastes far less at high current. For switching mains voltage or providing complete electrical isolation, use a relay or a solid state relay, with the transistor driving the relay's coil.
Billions of the same idea

The switch you can hold between two fingers is the same idea, in different form, as the ones in a processor. The first transistor was demonstrated at Bell Labs in December 1947 and was about the size of a thumb. A modern phone chip contains well over ten billion, each a switch turning the next one on or off. Logic gates, memory cells and arithmetic units are all arrangements of switches. Understand one transistor switching one LED and you hold the bottom rung of the ladder that leads to every computer.
